hints: Look at the shape of the graph and notice how water breaks the smooth trend seen for the other three hydrides.
Consider how boiling point rises from $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ to $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$ to $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$ due to increasing London dispersion forces with more electrons.
Think about what extra strong intermolecular force only small, highly electronegative atoms like O bonded to H can create.
walkthrough:
**Read the trend for the heavier hydrides**

Look at $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$. Their boiling points increase smoothly down the group.

This is expected because larger molecules have more electrons, so London dispersion (van der Waals) forces get stronger.

**Spot the anomaly for water**

$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ should have the lowest boiling point if it followed the same trend, because it is the smallest with fewest electrons.

Instead it boils at about $100^{\circ}\text{C}$, far higher than the others.

**Explain with hydrogen bonding**

Water can form strong hydrogen bonds between molecules. O is small and very electronegative, and it is bonded directly to H.

$$\text{H}^{\delta+} - \text{O}^{\delta-} \cdots \text{H}^{\delta+} - \text{O}^{\delta-}$$

Much more energy is needed to break these extra strong attractions, so the boiling point is anomalously high. S, Se and Te are too large and not electronegative enough for effective hydrogen bonding.

options.A: Shielding of nuclear charge affects atomic size and ionisation energy, not boiling point directly. Boiling depends on forces between molecules, not on electrons shielding within one atom.
options.B: Correct. Only water has extensive hydrogen bonding. This is a much stronger intermolecular force than the London dispersion forces between $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, $\text{H}_2\text{Se}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{Te}$, so much more heat energy is needed to separate the molecules and boil water.
options.C: Boiling does not break strong covalent O-H bonds inside the molecule. It only overcomes weak intermolecular forces between molecules. So covalent bond strength cannot explain the high boiling point.
options.D: Smaller molecules actually have weaker van der Waals (London dispersion) forces because they have fewer electrons and a smaller electron cloud. Water is small, so its dispersion forces are weakest, not strongest.
